title: Practical tactics to build reliable AI apps — Dmitry Kuchin, Multinear

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central focus is evaluation design, benchmark construction, LLM-as-judge, and regression testing methodology for AI applications. The evaluation methodology is explicitly cross-domain, with examples spanning support bots, text-to-SQL, classifiers, and guardrails. Covers the full journey from a 50%-working POC through benchmark-driven iteration to confident production deployment. Requires familiarity with generative AI development and the standard software development lifecycle as stated prerequisites. A 10-minute lightning talk with a live platform demonstration at a practitioner conference. All seven evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct character-range excerpts from the transcript.

summary: Dmitry Kuchin opens by establishing credibility: roughly 15 years as a startup co-founder/CTO, five years in enterprise executive roles, and the last couple of years building generative AI projects from POC to production. He frames the core problem: the standard software lifecycle (design, develop, test, deploy) breaks down with AI because models are non-deterministic, so a POC that works 50% of the time is easy, but achieving the remaining 50% is hard and demands continuous experimentation across prompts, models, data, and logic. He argues that teams misuse data-science metrics (groundedness, factuality, bias) because these abstractions do not reflect whether the solution actually serves users. He gives a Twilio customer-support example where the real signal is escalation rate to human support, not factuality. His prescription is to reverse engineer metrics from product and business outcomes, using capable models like o3 to generate realistic user questions and specific pass/fail criteria from source materials (e.g., a bank FAQ covering password reset with SMS validation). He stresses building evaluations at the very beginning, inspecting individual test failures rather than average scores, and iterating to establish a trusted benchmark. This benchmark then enables confident experimentation (switching models, simplifying logic, trying graph RAG or agentic approaches) while catching regressions. He notes evaluation strategies differ by solution type: LLM-as-judge for support bots, mock databases for text-to-SQL/text-to-graph, simple rubric matching for call-center classifiers, and targeted negative tests for guardrails. He closes by mentioning Multinear, his open-source platform, and a new startup focused on reliable AI automation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Build product-specific evaluations at the start of development, not the end, and iterate them alongside the solution.
Avoid generic data-science metrics (groundedness, factuality, bias); they do not capture whether users actually get what they need.
Reverse engineer evaluation criteria from real product and business outcomes, e.g., escalation rate for support bots rather than abstract factuality.
Use capable models like o3 to generate realistic user questions and precise pass/fail checklists from source materials.
Inspect individual test failures, not averages, to understand why a solution breaks and to guide targeted changes.
Establish a trusted benchmark before experimenting with model swaps, architecture simplifications, or agentic approaches, so regressions are caught.
Choose evaluation strategy by solution type: LLM-as-judge for support, mock databases for text-to-SQL, rubric matching for classifiers, negative tests for guardrails.
Frequent evaluation runs enable rapid progress with fewer regressions and effectively yield explainable AI behavior.

sections.title: Speaker introduction and credibility
sections.summary: Kuchin introduces himself, citing 15 years as a startup co-founder/CTO, five years in enterprise executive roles, and recent focus on generative AI projects from POC to production, claiming to have distilled a method for making AI applications reliable that others at the conference are not discussing.

sections.title: Why AI breaks the standard software lifecycle
sections.summary: Contrasts the standard design-develop-test-deploy cycle with AI development, where non-deterministic models make a 50%-working POC easy but the remaining reliability hard, requiring continuous experimentation across prompts, models, data, and logic.

sections.title: Wrong approach: generic data-science metrics
sections.summary: Critiques teams that default to groundedness, factuality, and bias metrics. Uses a Twilio support-bot anecdote to show the real metric is escalation rate to human support, not abstract factuality, and that universal metrics do not capture product-specific success.

sections.title: Reverse engineering product-specific evaluations
sections.summary: Advocates starting from real-world scenarios and using capable models like o3 to reverse engineer user questions and precise pass/fail criteria from source materials, illustrated with a bank FAQ password-reset example requiring SMS validation and fallback to support.

sections.title: Multinear platform demonstration
sections.summary: Shows the open-source Multinear platform displaying a password-reset question with input, output, and a specific checklist, noting the approach matters more than the tool and that he can recreate it quickly with Cursor.

sections.title: Evaluation-first process and benchmark building
sections.summary: Describes building evaluations at the start, inspecting individual failures, iterating until a trusted benchmark exists, then using it to confidently experiment with model swaps, graph RAG, agentic approaches, or logic simplification while catching regressions.

sections.title: Evaluation strategies by solution type
sections.summary: Explains that evaluation methods vary by solution: LLM-as-judge for support bots, mock databases for text-to-SQL or text-to-graph, simple rubric matching for call-center classifiers, and negative/edge-case tests for guardrails.

sections.title: Key takeaways and closing
sections.summary: Recaps: evaluate apps the way users use them, avoid abstract metrics, test frequently to catch regressions, and gain effectively explainable AI. Mentions Multinear is open source and that he is working on a reliable AI automation startup.

demonstrations: Multinear open-source platform showing a password-reset question with input, output, and specific criteria checklist used to judge correctness
